Rwanda return hubs in focus as higher Interior Ministry budget accepted
articles.body:
Plans foreseeing a rise of €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in the budget for the Interior Ministry have been approved by the three parties in Germany's coalition government, after much debate centering on something that makes up a relatively small proportion of that money: the controversial planned centers for rejected asylum seekers in Rwanda.

According to Klaus-Peter Willsch of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), just €5 million are earmarked for the so-called return hubs, shared between several European countries.

He said the €20 million that has often been cited as being for the Rwanda migration centers was not only for the hubs in that country, but for other potential projects in third countries as well.

Despite the relatively small amounts of money involved, the Rwanda plans devised by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) along with Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece came under fire not only from coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) but particularly from opposition parties.

The Green Party and the Left Party both rejected the idea for ethical reasons, with Green lawmaker Leon Eckert speaking of "state-organized human trafficking," while Dietmar Bartsch of the Left pointed out that the deal was being made with an authoritarian regime.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), for its part, said it found the plans too soft, with parliamentarian Marcus Bühl calling them a "smoke screen," as just 20 rejected asylum-seekers from Germany were to be initially sent to Rwanda under the scheme.

Dobrindt defended the scheme, saying that the opposition was trying to stir up controversy about a concept that had been approved at European level. He also called criticism of the political system in Rwanda inappropriate, citing a school for Afghan girls that had been set up in the country amid the ban on secondary education for females by the Taliban government.

The interior minister also praised the additional funds given to his ministry as a contribution to Germany's defense against hybrid attacks from Russia, with a rise in the budgets of both the IT security and the civic protection departments.

The draft 2027 budget, which was approved by the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the SPD, however includes less funding for the BAMF migration authority (from €999 million in 2026 to €994 million) and for integration aid for migrants and refugees (down €328 million to €1.07 billion).

German Foreign MinisterJohann Wadephul has warned against an expansion of the Ukraine conflict into other regions after the Ukrainian attacks on Russian ships in Libya.

Wadephul also condemned reported Russian attacks on two foreign freight ships said to be carrying grain near Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, saying such attacks did not concern only the security of nearby nations but also the food security of people in the Global South.

"It is clear that we cannot accept drone attacks on trading vessels," he said. "NATO will therefore step up its engagement in the region."

articles.title: Trial of alleged Russian spy delayed over health issues
articles.body:
The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman due to go on trial on Thursday on charges of spying for Russia was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

It was not clear whether her trial could go ahead as planned.

The 57-year-old woman has been accused of passing information to an officer from Russia's GRU intelligence agency who was posing as a diplomat at the Russian Embassy in Berlin.

Prosecutors allege that she used contacts with current and former German Defense Ministry officials to collect information on military aid for Ukraine, drone test sites and the arms industry.

She also faces accusation of having provided her alleged handler access to key political events in Berlin.

The woman was arrested in late January, with the alleged involvement of the Russian Embassy causing considerable outrage in Berlin.

Russia's ambassador was summoned over the incident, and the handler — identified by news weekly Der Spiegel as the embassy's deputy military attache — was expelled from Germany.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has rejected claims that Tehran was behind the drone attack on Kuwait that killed two Italians and injured two other people.

articles.body:
The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman charged with spying for Russia began in Berlin.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses.

Several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys said their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

articles.title: Russia says EU budget plans would prolong war in Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia has criticized the European Union's proposed seven-year budget, accusing the bloc of seeking to prolong the war in Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia has criticized the European Union's proposed seven-year budget, accusing the bloc of seeking to prolong the war in Ukraine.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the EU's plans to allocate money for Ukraine in its budget would make Kyiv "less inclined toward a peace process and more determined to continue the war."

Peskov said the result would be more military spending, leaving less for governments to spend on school, hospitals and social facilities.

"This is not money for peace," Peskov said.

Support for Ukraine is among the key areas of discussion in the 2028-2034 budget which includes up to €100 billion for Ukraine, however diplomats say this figure falls well short of Kyiv's needs.

articles.title: Germany: 2 arrested, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.summary: Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests
articles.body: Germany 's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday said it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro- Iranian terrorist group. It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and said that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne , several hours' drive to the north. Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests. Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing. Prosecutors said the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization. They said that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran . Mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025." Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks." "On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The plan was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out." Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency , the BfV. More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation. Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention. One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it. The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran. These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9 , which caused property damage but no injuries. Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later . An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after , prompting heightened security across the Netherlands. In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March , not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism. Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.

articles.title: Berlin trial of woman suspected of spying for Russia set to start
articles.summary: A German-Ukrainian woman accused of spying for Russia goes on trial in Berlin on Thursday
articles.body:
A German-Ukrainian woman accused of spying for Russia goes on trial in Berlin on Thursday.

She is charged with providing an employee and secret agent at the Russian Embassy in Berlin with sensitive information.

The alleged spy is accused of tipping the man off about high intelligence-value events over a period of years and helping him to secure entry.

The dpa news agency reports that the Russian agent in question was the country's deputy military attache, who has since been expelled from Germany.

The woman had long been known as a pro-Russian networker in the Berlin area, having lived in the country for several decades.

The lawsuit against her from the federal prosecutor's office based in Karslruhe also alleges that she tried to "win over individuals from the Federal Defense Ministry and the weapons industry for her purposes."

She is accused of acting out of personal conviction, rather than, say, fear or blackmail. She was arrested in January this year.

The woman is accused of making contact with the Russian espionage asset as of October 2023 at the latest. Her most pressing task was to seek out information pertaining to German defense policy and the weapons industry, particularly in light of and where relevant to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.body:
Iran is under severe economic pressure to end the war, Zeidon al-Kinani, a founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, told Al Jazeera.

“For Iran, the war wouldn’t make sense any more. The budget is coming up and the economic pressure is severe against the Iranian economy. Many salaries in the public sector are already not being paid,” he said.

“More salaries will not be able to be paid if this war were to be continued. So it’s an indicator that the Iranian government is trying to add further pressure as the status quo can’t be normalised on their side,” he added.

Al-Kinani said Iran’s attacks on Gulf countries are an attempt to pressure them to push for an end to the war.

“Iran believes that the GCC has enough ability to advocate for the war to end. But in reality the US conducted this war by ignoring its partnerships with the GCC and ignoring what this war might mean economically to a region that provides so much natural resources to the global economy.”

articles.title: Botchorishvili Denies Discussions on Moving Russia Talks to Moscow or Tbilisi, Kobakhidze Says It’s a Possibility
articles.summary: Georgian Dream Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili says there's no agreement on moving the resumed Russia-Georgia dialogue to Moscow or Tbilisi
articles.body: Georgian Dream Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili says there's no agreement on moving the resumed Russia-Georgia dialogue to Moscow or Tbilisi, while Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said such a thing is possible after the Belarusian foreign minister suggested the talks may move to the "capitals" after the first meeting took place in Minsk. The remarks follow a November 19 meeting in Minsk, Belarus, between George Zurabashvili, Georgia’s first deputy foreign minister and newly appointed special representative for relations with Russia, and Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin. Following the meeting, Belarusian Foreign Minister Maxim Ryzhenkov suggested that the talks could move to Moscow and Tbilisi, citing "substantive negotiations" during the first meeting. Botchorishvili: No Proposal or Decision Speaking to Georgia’s Public Broadcaster on November 25, Botchorishvili said there was "neither a proposal nor a decision" to hold meetings in Moscow or Tbilisi and that the issue was not on the agenda, adding that she did not consider it appropriate to discuss such matters in advance. She also dismissed Ryzhenkov’s assessment that the Minsk meeting had resulted in significant progress in building mutual trust between Georgia and Russia. “The Belarusian side is not a party to these meetings and has no information about their substance or results,” Botchorishvili said, stressing that only Georgia and Russia could assess the outcome of the talks. “Whether further meetings are necessary or whether they should continue is for the parties to decide, not those who have no role in the substance or conduct of these meetings." 26/11/2026 - Kobakhidze Suggests Russia’s Import Restrictions May Be Linked With ‘Deep State’ While acknowledging Belarus’ role in facilitating the Minsk meeting, Botchorishvili stressed that no agreement had been reached on further talks. “There is no agreement whatsoever on the continuation of meetings or on further steps. If there is a need for another meeting, the parties will discuss where it would be best to hold it, taking into account the circumstances and specific needs,” she said. Asked whether Minsk would replace Prague as the venue for Georgian-Russian talks, Botchorishvili said no decision had been made on a permanent location. “It is not written anywhere that the meeting must necessarily take place in Prague or any other city. Minsk was proposed as the venue, and, of course, we had no objection to holding the meeting there. This changes nothing about the substance of the meeting,” she said. Kobakhidze: Meetings in Moscow and Tbilisi Pose No Risks Talking to journalists on November 26, Kobakhidze said meetings could take place in both Moscow and Tbilisi, arguing that holding talks in the two capitals would not undermine Georgia’s non-recognition policy toward occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia. “These meetings can, of course, also take place in Moscow and Tbilisi. If such an approach is adopted, it is fundamentally important that the meetings be held alternately in Moscow and Tbilisi,” Kobakhidze told reporters. Kobakhidze stressed that the format should not entail any risks concerning the non-recognition policy of Georgia's occupied territories or other issues. “Holding these meetings in Moscow and Tbilisi does not pose any risks,” he said. “The main thing is that not even a single gesture should cast a shadow over the non-recognition policy. Neither the placement of flags there nor the holding of meetings in Moscow and Tbilisi runs counter to the principle of non-recognition.” Renewed Russia-Georgia Dialogue The informal direct dialogue between Georgia and Russia, commonly known as the Abashidze-Karasin format, was launched in late 2012, with Tbilisi introducing the post of a “Special Representative for Relations with Russia” for that purpose. In its original design, the format was limited to addressing trade, economic, humanitarian, and cultural issues, as diplomatic relations remain cut off amid Russia’s continued occupation of Georgian territories and its recognition of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia as “independent states.” George Zurabashvili was appointed as Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s special representative for relations with Russia on October 21, filling a position that had been vacant since December 2025. He was also allowed to retain his post as the first deputy foreign minister. Zurabashvili’s appointment raised concerns among former Georgian diplomats, who warned of a “dangerous trend” and questioned whether the move could signal a de facto restoration of diplomatic relations with Moscow, while also pointing to what they saw as the expansion of the post’s limited mandate to include security issues as well. articles.title: Rama Responds to Protests With New Restrictions Ahead of Nationwide Demonstration: SP Approve Hefty Fines Despite Constitutional Court Ruling Against Them
articles.summary: The court partially upheld the complaint and said it would issue a final ruling soon
articles.body: Two days before a nationwide demonstration called by students and activists, Albania’s ruling Socialist majority approved legislation restricting the right to protest, introducing tougher penalties that could leave demonstrators facing both legal and financial consequences, even when taking part in peaceful gatherings. The protest has been called for November 28, a date of particular symbolic significance in Albania: the 114th anniversary of the country’s declaration of independence. However, as parliament debated the new legislation, it came as a breaking news that Albania’s Constitutional Court ruled against the fines and announced that it would fast-track its review of a complaint filed by students and opposition lawmakers. The court partially upheld the complaint and said it would issue a final ruling soon. But the ruling Socialists said they would press ahead with the legislative changes despite the Constitutional Court’s decision. The government adopted two emergency acts on October 28, 2026, amid a wave of mass demonstrations that have repeatedly erupted into clashes with police. Normative Act amends Albania’s Law on Public Gatherings, granting the State Police broader powers to intervene in demonstrations and prohibit protests. It also introduces administrative fines ranging from 10,000 to 500,000 Albanian lek (approximately $120 to $6,200). Albania is experiencing one of its most politically tense periods in more than a decade. Protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government, which began in late May, have continued almost daily in the capital, Tirana, for nearly six months. The demonstrations initially emerged in opposition to a luxury tourism development planned in Zvërnec, on Albania’s southern coast, by a group of investors led by Jared Kushner, the American businessman and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump. The project has drawn criticism because of its location in an environmentally protected coastal area. What began as a campaign against the development gradually expanded into a broader protest movement, attracting people angered by the rising cost of living, government arrogance, a lack of accountability and systemic corruption. The demonstrations intensified in October, when students joined the protests and began demanding Rama’s resignation. By mid-October, students had become a central force in the movement. They are demanding better conditions at public universities, lower tuition fees and meaningful action against corruption, which they say extends far beyond the education system. Many young protesters say they see little room for opportunity under Rama’s government and increasingly struggle to imagine a future for themselves in Albania. As confrontations escalated, police used force against students, including water cannons, tear gas and rubber bullets, in attempts to disperse demonstrations. Rama has refused to resign, despite continuing demands from protesters. Instead, his government has moved to tighten the legal framework governing public demonstrations. The prime minister has defended the changes as necessary to maintain public order and protect businesses affected by violence during protests. Journalists, activists and government critics, however, argue that the legislation risks being used to suppress a broader protest movement challenging the government at a politically sensitive moment. Under the amendments, police can prohibit or restrict demonstrations for up to three days in areas surrounding a wide range of public institutions. The Police can impose restrictions within designated areas around government buildings, educational institutions and healthcare facilities if authorities believe there is a risk of violence against people or damage to property. The restriction can be renewed for another three days, meaning a demonstration could effectively be banned for up to six consecutive days. Organizers have the right to challenge such decisions before an administrative court. However, a controversial provision means that even if the court rules in their favor, the police are not required to immediately implement the judgment. In practice, critics warn, the changes could make it considerably harder to organize demonstrations, including peaceful ones, because restrictions can be imposed on the basis of police assessments that a gathering might turn violent. In Tirana, where government offices, shcools, hospitals and major transport hubs are spread across the city, the restricted perimeters could potentially cover substantial parts of the capital. If officers identify social media posts they believe encourage violence in connection with the organization of a demonstration, they can demand that the content be removed and not repeated. The provision raises concerns about how the authorities will distinguish between genuine incitement to violence and legitimate political speech, criticism of the government or calls for peaceful demonstrations. Critics argue that the legislation gives police considerable discretion in determining what constitutes an online call for violence. The amendments significantly increase administrative penalties, with some fines reportedly rising by as much as tenfold compared with previous levels. According to the text of the legislation published by Albanian media, fines range from 10,000 to 500,000 lek, more than 5500 euros and eight times albanian middle wage. This means that participation in a demonstration could carry substantial financial risks, even in the absence of physical violence. The legislation has drawn criticism from activists, civil society organizations and opposition parties. Student groups, civil society organizations and opposition lawmakers have petitioned Albania’s Constitutional Court, asking it to repeal the amendments and suspend their implementation until a final ruling is issued. The Court ruled to suspend the article regarding fines for blocking roads. The court announced that it would fast-track its review of a complaint filed by students and opposition lawmakers. The court partially upheld the complaint and said it would issue a final ruling soon. More than 100 peaceful demonstrators have already been fined under the new legislation, according to Albanian media reports. Police have also initiated criminal proceedings against a large number of people, including minors.

articles.title: European Parliament adopts resolution on Georgia, calls for sanctions and release of political prisoners
articles.summary: The European Parliament reiterated its call for a coordinated EU response
articles.body: The European Parliament adopted a resolution on Georgia on November 26, calling for the immediate release of political prisoners and the imposition of targeted sanctions against senior Georgian officials. The resolution, titled “Case of Paata Burchuladze and political prisoners under the Georgian Dream regime,” was approved with 441 votes in favor, 47 against and 86 abstentions. The European Parliament reiterated its call for a coordinated EU response, including targeted sanctions and visa bans against individuals it holds responsible for serious human rights violations, specifically naming Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze, alongside other senior officials, judges, prosecutors and law enforcement personnel. MEPs condemned the sentences handed down to Paata Burchuladze, Irakli Nadiradze and Paata Manjgaladze, demanding their immediate and unconditional release, along with all individuals the resolution identifies as political prisoners or unlawfully detained. The document urges the Georgian authorities to uphold international fair trial standards, guarantee Burchuladze adequate medical care and legal assistance, facilitate regular communication with his family and ensure unrestricted consular access. The European Parliament further calls on the Georgian authorities to end what it describes as politically motivated prosecutions and judicial harassment of artists, opposition figures, journalists and activists, while guaranteeing freedom of expression, assembly and association. MEPs also demand independent investigations into allegations of excessive use of force, intimidation and ill-treatment of protesters, stressing the need to hold those responsible accountable. The resolution reaffirms the European Parliament’s support for the Georgian people and their democratic aspirations, emphasizing that respect for the rule of law, the European Convention on Human Rights and fundamental freedoms is essential for progress toward EU membership. MEPs also criticized the failure of some EU member states to take action against individuals they consider responsible for democratic backsliding in Georgia.

articles.title: Dodik after the Decision of the Constitutional Court: They Will Not Put Up a Single Flag of the Army of RBiH in RS
articles.summary: This is a constitutional right of the Serb people and Republika Srpska
articles.body: Milorad Dodik, president of the SNSD party, said that “not even 100 Constitutional Courts” will put up a single flag of the Army of RBiH in Republika Srpska, after the Constitutional Court ruled that the ban on displaying Army of RBiH insignia in the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska is unconstitutional. “If 100 Constitutional Courts appear, not a single one will put up the flag of the Army of RBiH in Republika Srpska; I dare them to try,” Dodik said at the press conference, RTRS reported. “This is a constitutional right of the Serb people and Republika Srpska. The will of the Serb people cannot be challenged,” Dodik said, adding that “there is no getting over this.” He called the decision of the Constitutional Court “a typical Muslim conspiracy theory to destroy Republika Srpska.” At the plenary session held on November 19 and 20, the Constitutional Court of BiH ruled that the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska is unconstitutional for criminalizing the public display, representation, and use of symbols and insignia that promote or glorify the Army of RBiH. Previously, the US filed an appeal regarding this ban, and the member of the Presidency of BiH, Denis Bećirović, submitted a request for a constitutionality assessment. In the same session, the Constitutional Court rejected the statement by Željka Cvijanović, the Serb member of the BiH Presidency, that Republika Srpska’s vital interest had been violated. It also rejected the decision by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska confirming that statement. Cvijanović vetoed the Decision of the Presidency of BiH to appoint members of the Commission for the Preservation of National Monuments, which had been made without consensus. This decision of the Presidency remains in force. The National Assembly of Republika Srpska banned displaying insignia of the Army of RBiH by amending the Criminal Code. The Constitutional Court of Republika Srpska has previously assessed that this law did not violate the vital national interest of the Bosniak people, N1 writes.

articles.title: European Parliament to vote on resolution concerning Paata Burchuladze and Georgian political prisoners
articles.summary: The European Parliament’s plenary agenda lists the resolution under procedure 2026/2992(RSP), with voting scheduled between 12:00 and 14:00 local time
articles.body: The European Parliament is set to vote today, November 26, on a draft resolution titled “The Case of Paata Burchuladze and Political Prisoners under the Georgian Dream Regime.” The voting session is scheduled to begin after 12:00 local time in Strasbourg (15:00 Tbilisi time), as indicated on the European Parliament’s official website. Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) debated the draft resolution on Wednesday, November 25, addressing the case of the internationally renowned Georgian opera singer Paata Burchuladze and the broader human rights situation in Georgia. The European Parliament’s plenary agenda lists the resolution under procedure 2026/2992(RSP), with voting scheduled between 12:00 and 14:00 local time. The draft resolution calls for the immediate and unconditional release of Burchuladze and other individuals whom its authors consider political prisoners, including opposition politicians Irakli Nadiradze and Paata Manjgaladze. The authors question the fairness of Burchuladze’s trial and raise concerns over his detention conditions, access to medical care and restrictions on communication with his family. They also urge the Georgian authorities to ensure unrestricted consular access, as Burchuladze holds both Georgian and Austrian citizenship. The proposed document calls for targeted EU sanctions against senior Georgian officials, including Georgian Dream founder Bidzina Ivanishvili, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze. Burchuladze, 71, was sentenced to seven years in prison in May 2026 in connection with the events of October 4, 2025, when a large anti-government demonstration coinciding with municipal elections culminated in an attempt by protesters to enter the presidential palace in Tbilisi. He faced charges including organizing group violence, attempting to seize a strategic facility and calling for the violent overthrow of the constitutional order. Burchuladze denies the charges. Georgian Dream has rejected the accusations of political persecution. Commenting on the draft resolution on Wednesday, ruling party MP Aluda Gudushauri dismissed the initiative as politically motivated and denied that it reflected the situation in Georgia. The vote comes amid increasingly strained relations between Tbilisi and Brussels, with European institutions repeatedly expressing concerns over democratic backsliding, judicial independence and fundamental freedoms in Georgia. Although European Parliament resolutions are not legally binding, they represent the institution’s political position and can increase pressure on EU institutions and member states to take further action. The vote has not yet taken place. The final wording of the resolution remains subject to parliamentary approval.

At least eight killed in Nigerian bus fire
articles.summary: The bus was reportedly speeding at the time
articles.body: At least eight people were killed and five others rescued after a bus caught fire in Nigeria's southwestern Lagos State Thursday, local authorities said, Xinhua reports. Olufemi Damilola Oke-Osanyintolu, head of the Lagos State Emergency Management Agency, told local media that the bus, which was carrying at least 13 people, including the driver, crashed into a road culvert and burst into flames along the Lagos-Badagry Expressway. The bus was reportedly speeding at the time. The official attributed the incident to "excessive speeding and reckless driving," citing preliminary police investigations. He said emergency responders rescued five adults, who were taken to a government hospital for medical attention. Fatal road accidents are common in Nigeria and are often attributed to speeding, overloading, poor road conditions, and reckless driving.

articles.title: Two police officers killed in southwestern Colombia armed attack
articles.summary: Stronger protective measures were ordered in the municipality
articles.body: Two police officers were killed and four others injured in an armed attack in Padilla in Colombia's southwestern department of Cauca, the National Police said Wednesday. The officers, who were escorting municipal government officials, were patrolling a rural area of Padilla when the attack occurred, according to a social media post by the National Police. Stronger protective measures were ordered in the municipality. The National Police said coordinated security operations were underway to identify and apprehend those responsible for the attack.

articles.title: Ten killed, four injured after truck plunges into river in Uganda
articles.summary: Unfortunately, when it reached River Nyagak, the driver lost control of the vehicle at the bridge and plunged into the river
articles.body: At least 10 people were killed and four others seriously injured after a truck plunged into a river in the northwestern Ugandan district of Zombo Thursday, a police spokesperson said, Xinhua reports. The truck, which was carrying sacks of cassava flour and traders returning from a local market, lost control at Nyagak Bridge and plunged into the River Nyagak at around 10:00 a.m. local time (GMT 0700), Josephine Angucia, West Nile regional police spokesperson, said in a statement. "Unfortunately, when it reached River Nyagak, the driver lost control of the vehicle at the bridge and plunged into the river. Police responded to the scene to help the victims and survivors and to manage the scene professionally," Angucia said. The four seriously injured, two men and two women, were rushed to hospital for treatment, she said. Divers were still searching the river for other people and bodies believed to be trapped underwater, Angucia added.

articles.summary: A person with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters that no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were ​accessed

articles.summary: Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae arrives for work at the Supreme Court in Seoul, Tuesday
articles.body: Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae arrives for work at the Supreme Court in Seoul, Tuesday. Yonhap An international legal association voiced concern over the ruling party's push to impeach the chief justice, urging extreme caution to safeguard judicial independence. In a statement released Thursday, the Law Association for Asia and the Pacific (LAWASIA), acknowledged the constitutional legitimacy of impeachment but stressed the need to uphold fundamental democratic principles. "LAWASIA acknowledges that impeachment is a remedy recognized by the Constitution of the Republic of Korea, and that no person or institution is above the law," the statement read. "LAWASIA emphasises, however, that any action taken by government against the courts must be exercised with extreme caution." LAWASIA represents legal professionals and leading legal associations across some 40 jurisdictions in the Asia-Pacific region. The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) plans to seek the impeachment of Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae as early as next week. The grounds cited for impeachment include the court's handling of President Lee Jae Myung's election law case, its response to the December 2024 martial law crisis, disputes over judicial appointments and Cho's refusal to testify before the National Assembly. The grounds for impeachment have been disputed, with some critics describing the move as an attempt to silence the judiciary. Any impeachment proceedings must "respect and observe fundamental democratic principles, including the separation of powers and judicial independence," according to the statement. The statement also warned of the potential erosion of public trust in the legal system. "LAWASIA hopes that tensions between the government and the courts can be resolved through constructive dialogue rather than action which risks undermining public confidence in the legal system." LAWASIA adopted the Beijing Principles of the Independence of the Judiciary in 1997, a set of guidelines signed by chief justices from 32 Asia-Pacific countries to safeguard judicial independence. Under Principle 22, judges should be removed from office only on established grounds, such as incapacity, criminal conviction or conduct that makes them unfit to serve. In addition, principle 23 acknowledges that some legal systems allow judges to be removed through parliamentary proceedings but warns that such procedures risk being misused unless reserved for the most serious cases.

articles.summary: To prevent a legal vacuum, however, the court kept the clause in effect until it can be revised, no later than Dec
articles.body: Justices take their seats to deliver rulings on requests for constitutional review and constitutional complaints in the Constitutional Court's courtroom in Jongno District, Seoul, Thursday. Yonhap The Constitutional Court ruled Thursday that a provision of the Immigration Act imposing a general ban on political activity by foreign residents does not conform to the Constitution, with six of the nine judges agreeing. To prevent a legal vacuum, however, the court kept the clause in effect until it can be revised, no later than Dec. 31, 2028. The provision was introduced in 1977. A 2005 amendment added an exception for political activities permitted under other laws, but the general ban stayed in place. Violators can be ordered to halt the activity or leave the country and those without permanent resident status may face deportation. In 2021, two Mongolian international students planned to request preliminary candidates in the 20th presidential election present policies to address discrimination against foreign nationals living in Korea. They filed a constitutional complaint that July after learning the law barred them from political activity. The court found that freedom of expression, unlike voting and other political rights, is a constitutional right that applies to both citizens and foreign nationals. It said restricting political activity to protect national security and the sovereignty of the Korean people is a legitimate legislative goal, but the law failed to define the scope of banned activities. The court noted that separate laws restrict election campaigning, party membership and political donations by foreign nationals. Other provisions of the Immigration Act can also regulate activities that threaten the country's security or public order, it said. The court said Germany's approach of generally allowing political activity by foreign nationals while listing prohibited acts in law is another option. It also took into account that the United States and Japan have no separate provision in their immigration laws broadly banning such activity.

articles.summary: The Prime Minister-designate for the new Government of Republika Srpska (RS), Igor Dodik, expects social partners to reach an agreement through dialogue
articles.body: While trade unions seek a 12 to 14 per cent minimum wage increase, employers believe a four to five per cent increase is realistic at this point. The Prime Minister-designate for the new Government of Republika Srpska (RS), Igor Dodik, expects social partners to reach an agreement through dialogue. Following today’s consultation with the union representatives, business community, employers, and entrepreneurs, Dodik said the talks were constructive and produced good proposals. He emphasised that the new Government will continue working to improve citizens’ material standing, raise wages, and preserve the positive employment trend, stating that the number of employed in Republika Srpska has reached a record high of more than 292,000. “Social dialogue and cooperation between the trade unions and employers are very important. I believe they will agree on the minimum wage as well, without the government having to impose a final solution,” Dodik said. According to him, employers propose a four to five per cent increase, while the trade union demands growth of 12 to 14 per cent. Regarding the general collective agreement, Dodik said that certain measures have already been taken, but that some questions require reaching a compromise with the Union of Employers. He also announced that, if needed, the Labour Law could also be reopened to reach a general collective agreement that would protect the rights of all employees, especially in the real sector. Dodik said that the Government will prioritise easing the burden on the economy, combating the grey economy, attracting foreign investments, and increasing employment. He especially emphasised the need to curb cash-in-envelope wage payments, announcing that public institutions will further work on identifying employers who do not pay full salaries and that penalties for such violations should be increased. As one of the priorities of the future Government, he also singled out responsible management of public enterprises. “We heard today that a situation in certain enterprises and public institutions is not very great. If we determine certain things, and if I am elected prime minister, I will demand a report on all those operations at one of the first government sessions,” Dodik said. He added that accountability will be sought from executives found to have caused damage or not respond to business challenges.

articles.title: Uzbekistan presents disability rights experience at CIS meeting
articles.body: Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan presented its experience in protecting the rights of persons with disabilities at the seventh meeting of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Human Rights Commission, held in Minsk. Uzbekistan was represented by Mirzatillo Tillabayev, a member of the Commission and First Deputy Director of the National Human Rights Centre of Uzbekistan. The meeting was chaired by Yevgenia Paramonova, Belarus's representative to the CIS Human Rights Commission and Head of the Main Directorate for Criminal and Judicial Supervision at the Prosecutor General's Office of Belarus. Representatives of Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan took part in the meeting in a hybrid format, alongside representatives of the CIS Executive Committee and its structural divisions. Participants heard country reports on the observance of the rights of persons with disabilities in the Commission's member states. The reports were timed to coincide with the CIS Year of Healthcare and the 20th anniversary of the UN General Assembly's adoption of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities on 13 December 2006. Tillabayev outlined Uzbekistan's experience in ensuring and protecting the rights of persons with disabilities. He addressed constitutional guarantees in this area, implementation of the Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the implementation of the UN Convention. Participants showed particular interest in information on the implementation of the action plan marking the Convention's 20th anniversary. They also heard about a special session entitled "20 Years of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities: From Recognition of Rights to Inclusive Societies", scheduled to take place as part of the Fifth Samarkand Human Rights Forum. The Commission also discussed the right to health, in connection with the CIS Year of Healthcare, and the rights of women in the penitentiary system. It reviewed the results of the "Right to Health" creative competition and considered ways to strengthen cooperation on safeguarding the rights and freedoms of migrant workers and their family members, as well as protecting and promoting the rights of older people. Igor Petrishenko, First Deputy Secretary General of the CIS, said that over 35 years the Commonwealth had developed a system of multilateral agreements that formed the basis for interstate dialogue, along with effective cooperation mechanisms covering a wide range of issues. He highlighted cooperation in legal and humanitarian matters, including the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. During Belarus's 2026 chairmanship, the Commission focused on educational and awareness-raising activities. These included the "Week of Health and Human Rights in the CIS", linked to the Sustainable Development Goals, and the "Right to Health" creative competition, which received hundreds of entries. The meeting approved the Commission's work plan for the coming year, taking into account the designation of 2027 as the CIS Year of Legal Awareness.

articles.title: Zelenskyy warns Russia preparing ‘new massive strike’ as Ukraine seeks urgent air defence supplies
articles.body:
Turning briefly to Ukraine, president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Russia is preparing for a “new massive strike” against the country, with energy facilities, logistics infrastructure and essential services expected to be among the targets.

“Unfortunately, the Russians are already completing preparations for a new massive strike,” Zelensky wrote on X.

He said Ukrainian intelligence indicated that the country’s energy infrastructure would again be a primary target, as repair crews continue working around the clock to restore electricity supplies following Russian attacks on “substations, overhead power lines, and the entire power grid”.

Zelensky added that he was awaiting an update from Ukraine’s foreign ministry on discussions with international partners over additional air defence supplies, adding that interceptor missiles for Patriot and Nasams systems were a “key priority”.

His warning comes as EU leaders meet in Brussels to discuss continued financial support for Ukraine, alongside negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget. The European Commission has proposed a further €45bn loan for Kyiv in 2027, but member states remain divided over how the money should be provided, with Germany pushing for the entire bloc to participate (see post at 9.15am).

In a video address yesterday, Zelenskyy said there was “no good news” from the US on accelerating air defence deliveries, saying they were “still delayed”.

articles.title: Russia slams NATO chief Rutte for Vietnam War analogy on battlefield losses
articles.body:
Russian Security Council Secretary Sergei Shoigu accused NATO chief Mark Rutte of applying double standards in his assessment of Russian casualties in Ukraine, pointing to civilian deaths during the Vietnam War.

In a keynote speech earlier this month, Rutte compared NATO estimates of Russian losses in Ukraine with US casualties during the 14-year Vietnam War.

"In the past few months, Russia has been losing more than 40,000 troops – killed or seriously wounded – every month," Rutte said. "The United States in 14 years, in Vietnam, lost 56,000."

Shoigu hit back in a statement published on Telegram, saying the NATO chief had "sheepishly omitted the fact that the conflict instigated by the US claimed the lives of an estimated 3.4 million Vietnamese, more than 2 million of whom were civilians"

Russia has not given an official death toll among its army since September 2022, when it said almost 6,000 soldiers had been killed in the first six months of fighting – a figure widely seen as a large undercount even at the time.

The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, has acknowledged that leaders remain “very far apart,” agreeing with Germany’s Merz that the current proposal is not going to work.

Just like Martin earlier, she noted that 2027 will see “very important political elections across the member state” and openly acknowledged that “the situation within Europe could become even more challenging” as a result, making it important to get a deal this year.

Frederiksen also backed Merz’s call to link the funding for with the new budget, saying Ukraine serves as “Europe’s first line of defence.”

“If Ukraine falls, I believe there is a significant risk … that Russia might push further,” she warned.

She added that “in Europe, we have a tradition of collectively financing our shared expenses, and we must view the funding for Ukraine as part of that.”

Interestingly, she was also asked if the EU would be able to continue this support for Ukraine given several elections in the next 12 months, which could see rightwing and far-right parties come to power in France, Spain and Poland, among others.

She replied candidly that she didn’t know, but strongly “cautioned” against thinking that Europe could simply stop supporting Ukraine and spend the money elsewhere.

“Given everything we are seeing from the Russian side right now … if we let Ukraine fall, we essentially open the door for Russia to advance further,” she said.

editorialRejections.body: Moldovan president says Russia does not want to end war President Maia Sandu believes that drones entering the country’s airspace represent both a consequence of the intensification of Russian attacks on Ukraine and the result of deliberate actions aimed at testing the authorities’ response and intimidating the population. The head of state said that, in her opinion, Russia currently does not want to end the war in Ukraine and that pressure on Moscow must increase, in order to improve the chances of peace. She made statements to this effect today evening at the Secrets of Power programme, broadcast on Jurnal TV, in the context of recent incidents in which more drones entered the airspace of Moldova. Referring to the recorded cases, including the one of a drone that flew over Chisinau from north to south and reached the area of the international airport, Maia Sandu said there had been more explanations for these incidents. “I believe it is a combination. Of course, the increase in the number of cases is determined by the increase in the number of attacks on Ukraine, because we see what a terrible situation is unfolding there, and when the regions bordering Moldova are targeted, drones also reach us. But it is clear that, in some cases, there are also deliberate actions, or actions that test our response and seek to intimidate us. It is not only Moldova’s case. You saw what happened in Poland a few days ago,” the head of state said. According to Maia Sandu, the intensification of Russian attacks on Ukraine and actions affecting other countries as well increase the risks for the citizens of Moldova. “This is a more advanced level of aggression on the part of the Russian Federation, primarily toward Ukraine, in terms of what it is doing to cities and villages and to civilians, but also toward other states. Obviously, the greater the number, the greater the risk for our citizens,” the president said. In the same context, Maia Sandu referred to what she described as a paradox between diplomatic efforts to stop the war and the intensification of military actions. “We are somehow living through a paradox on this period. There is a great deal of discussion about peace. Some meetings are taking place in neutral locations. We hear all sorts of promises that peace is just around the corner. At the same time, however, the war is growing in scale. There are powerful strikes that carry great weight, both literally and figuratively, from both sides,” the head of state said. Asked whether international efforts could lead to a ceasefire and the restoration of peace, the president said that, in her opinion, Russia is not interested in stopping the war. “It is true that efforts are being made to reach a ceasefire and restore peace. The problem is that Russia does not want this. That is my opinion. Based on what I have seen and heard, I do not believe that Putin wants to stop this war. If he wanted to, they are the ones who could stop it, and there would be no more war,” Maia Sandu said. The head of state noted that American and European partners were making diplomatic efforts, but she believes these will not produce results, as long as Moscow does not want to end the war. “The partners, both the Americans and the Europeans, are of course trying and holding discussions. I do not believe that these actions will lead to results, because Russia, under Putin’s regime, does not want to stop the war. I believe it will exploit this winter,” the president said. In her opinion, increasing pressure on Moscow, including through sanctions and measures affecting the Russian economy, is necessary to improve the chances of peace. “To enhance the chances of peace, pressure on Moscow must be increased. This means sanctions; Russia’s economy must be weakened, because as long as the economy can generate resources, they will be directed toward producing even more military equipment, more ballistic missiles, drones and so on, which are used to kill people in Ukraine,” Maia Sandu said. The president also said that, in her opinion, the Russian authorities were trying to create the impression that they are interested in peace negotiations, while continuing their attacks on Ukraine. “I do not believe that the regime in Moscow is genuinely interested in these peace talks at this time. I believe they are only trying to create the impression that they are interested in these discussions, but in reality, they will continue doing what they have done until now: brutally attacking Ukraine,” the head of state concluded. editorialRejections.body: Constanța, Romania – Out on the Black Sea, the Romanian Navy is always on the lookout for the deadly debris of a war it isn't fighting.It's a front of the Russia-Ukraine war that most people rarely see. It runs right up to NATO's doorstep and sometimes crosses into its waters — threatening to pull the alliance, and therefore the United States, into the war.Incidents involving drones, mines and commercial ships are surging in the Black Sea, NATO military spokesperson Colonel Martin O'Donnell told CBS News."In 2025, for example, we saw fewer than 50 incidents in the Black Sea. This year alone, we're talking four to five hundred," he said.The roughly tenfold increase threatens a major artery of global grain and fuel shipments and has made the waterway deadlier than the Strait of Hormuz, a flashpoint in the U.S.-Iran war, with both sides trying to enforce blockades on the chokepoint to exert economic pressure on the other.Twenty-five sailors have been killed in the strait this year, according to the International Maritime Organization, while at least 40 have been killed in the Black Sea in the same period, according to the International Transport Workers' Federation."I would say the Black Sea is just as important, and then depending on who you talk to, some might argue could perhaps even be more important … in terms of global trade," said O'Donnell.Any imbalance in the flow of fuel and food "can have global implications that can impact America just as much as it can any of the nations here," he said.And this maritime front stretches beyond the Black Sea.Over the weekend, Ukraine said it struck an advanced Russian warship and a cargo ship that then drifted, on fire, into the waters of NATO member Finland.On Sunday, Ukraine said it sank a Russian warship docked in Libya.Three of the six countries bordering the Black Sea are NATO members — Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey.But as Romanian Navy Captain Mihai Iordache explains, defending those borders is nothing like defending them on land."We do not have a fence into the Black Sea to state this is our border, that is the other border," he said.The Romanian Navy is deploying highly specialized divers and drones, scouring the depths for unexploded weapons.All this comes as the pressure on NATO is mounting. On Friday, Poland accused Russia of "intentional provocation" as Russian cruise missiles landed in the country's southeast. Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.Asked whether the alliance will defend itself if necessary, O'Donnell told CBS News: "I would say that there should be no doubt on NATO's willingness and ability to act."On the Black Sea, Captain Iordache warns the Romanian Navy is already stretched thin."We don't have enough people, personnel, equipment to deal with all the commercial ships and all the drones that we have," he told CBS News during an embed."Four years ago, we were ready for one drifting mine, and right now we are ready for tens of drifting drones," he said. "So I presume we'll be ready in the future, who knows what the future will bring." "Could be hotter, could be colder, who knows. Let's hope for peace."

editorialRejections.body: Raphaël Glucksmann, the Social Democrats' candidate for the French presidency, has responded to remarks by potential election rival and judoka Teddy Riner, who said that the war in Ukraine is not his country's war. Source: French news broadcast television and radio network BFMTV, as reported by European Pravda Details: Responding to Riner's remarks, Glucksmann said that the war in Ukraine "determines our future" and that those who want to stop providing aid to Kyiv are acting against France's vital interests. "The war in Ukraine is our war, because it will determine our future, because we are Vladimir Putin's targets," the Social Democratic Party candidate said. He noted that the war in Ukraine extends far beyond its borders, as Russia is also waging a war against Europe. Glucksmann added that those who oppose helping Ukraine are betraying France. "Anyone who calls for an end to aid for the Ukrainian resistance is calling for submission to the tyrant who seeks to undermine European security. They are therefore acting against France's vital interests. If we do that, we are betraying France; we are betraying Europe," the politician stressed. Glucksmann was responding to remarks by judoka Teddy Riner, who is also running for president and said on Wednesday that Ukraine's war is "not our war". Riner later told AFP that he wants to stop "giving away money we don't have" to support Kyiv. Background: Marine Le Pen, the informal leader of the far-right National Rally, has pledged to stop funding Ukraine if elected president. She has also confirmed that she does not plan to cancel military aid to Ukraine. In October, Le Pen said she is ready to visit Ukraine for a debate with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on financial assistance.

"An assessment we conducted about a year ago showed that this amounts to participation in the war. If anything has changed, I will let you know, but that is what I know from discussions within Romanian state institutions at the time," he said. On November 20, Wirtualna Polska, citing Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, reported that two missiles and a drone entered Polish airspace on Friday morning and fell in two eastern Polish regions. No one was injured. On November 23, NATO announced the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft in Poland following the incident and blamed Russia for it. Russian Ambassador to Poland Georgy Mikhno dismissed allegations of Russian involvement in the November 20 incidents, which were described as violations of Polish airspace, calling them baseless and unsupported by evidence.

editorialRejections.body: US President Donald Trump is testing Russian President Vladimir Putin to determine whether he is ready for genuine negotiations, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said, according to the German news agency dpa.In an interview with Fox News ahead of his meeting with Trump at the US president's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Wednesday, November 25, the NATO secretary-general said that the American leader was testing Putin. As an example, he pointed to last week's meeting between Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. According to Rutte, the US president is asking the Russian leader direct questions about his intentions. Is he willing to come to the negotiating table? Is he willing to really engage in talks? the NATO secretary general said, describing Trump's approach. Rutte believes that this approach and pressure on Russia must be maintained. I think it is working, and we have to keep that going, he stressed. Meanwhile, the German news agency dpa notes that Trump's dealings with Putin frequently draw criticism. The US administration positions itself more as a mediator in efforts to end the war Russia started than as a supporter of Ukraine. Trump's recent remarks during his visit to China, when he referred to Putin as his friend, also sparked outrage. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously responded to this rhetoric and criticized what he considers insufficient pressure from Washington on the Kremlin. In an interview with CNN a few days ago, he stressed that such remarks undermine efforts to exert pressure on Putin. Zelenskyy said that when Putin is spoken of like he's a friend, or he is something like this, he does not feel that he is a killer. He doesn't feel enough pressure, the Ukrainian president emphasized. US President Donald Trump has recently demonstrated a willingness to pursue unconventional diplomatic engagement with authoritarian leaders. In particular, the American leader unexpectedly recalled his love letters with Kim Jong Un and hinted at renewed talks, suggesting that their correspondence from his first term could resume. Meanwhile, Trump's rhetoric on ending the war in Ukraine remains contradictory. Trump previously laughed off Zelenskyy's remarks about reaching a deal with Russia by January, responding sarcastically to the Ukrainian president's statement about Washington's desire to reach an agreement within a short timeframe. This stance has sparked debate among Western allies over how much pressure Washington is actually exerting on the Kremlin.

editorialRejections.title: Maia Sandu denies talks on Moldova's federalization in Ukraine negotiations, stating no source has confirmed it President Maia Sandu has dismissed reports that Russia is seeking to include the federalization of the Republic of Moldova in discussions on ending the war in Ukraine. She said no official source involved in the talks had confirmed the scenarios and stressed that the country's territorial integrity is not up for negotiation.
editorialRejections.reason: Routine, incomplete or malformed headline outside the DNU brief
editorialRejections.body: President Maia Sandu has dismissed reports that Russia is seeking to include the federalization of the Republic of Moldova in discussions on ending the war in Ukraine. She said no official source involved in the talks had confirmed the scenarios and stressed that the country's territorial integrity is not up for negotiation. President Maia Sandu has dismissed reports circulating in the public sphere about a purported “roadmap” proposed by Moscow that would envisage the federalization of the Republic of Moldova into three entities: the Republic of Moldova, the Gagauz Autonomous Territorial Unit, and the Transnistrian region. According to these reports, the entities would be granted the right to hold independence referendums if the Republic of Moldova joined the European Union, following the Kozak Memorandum model. “This has not been discussed; therefore, the information has not been confirmed by any source among those who participated in these discussions. Of course, it would not come as a great surprise if, at some point, the Russians were to propose such a thing, given that they clearly lack respect for states in the region and beyond. We could, with equal justification, suggest that they hold a referendum in Chechnya,” the President said during a show on Jurnal TV. Maia Sandu assured that international partners firmly support the sovereignty and internationally recognized borders of the Republic of Moldova, ruling out any possibility of the country's status becoming a subject of negotiation. “Everyone, with the exception of Russia, respects the territorial integrity of the Republic of Moldova. There is simply no way our status could end up on the negotiating table,” the head of state concluded. Russian and German media reported that, according to sources involved in trilateral negotiations between Russia, Ukraine, and the U.S.—held in Abu Dhabi on November 11–12 regarding an end to the war in Ukraine—Moscow allegedly proposed transforming the Republic of Moldova into a federal state, composed of Moldova proper, the Transnistrian region, and the Autonomous Territorial Unit of Gagauzia. Furthermore, should the Republic of Moldova join the European Union, referendums on the independence of these territories would be held. In exchange, Russia would agree to withdraw its troops from the left bank of the Nistru, provided that the Republic of Moldova adopts a status of military non-alignment. The idea of ​​federalizing the Republic of Moldova is not new. One of the most well-known proposals was the 2003 Kozak Memorandum, which envisioned transforming the country into an asymmetric federation consisting of three entities: the Republic of Moldova, the Transnistrian region, and Gagauzia. The document, drafted by Dmitry Kozak—then deputy chief of the Kremlin’s Presidential Administration—stipulated a bicameral parliament in which representatives from the Transnistrian region and Gagauzia would have held significant weight. The proposed structure would have granted representatives from Tiraspol the ability to influence decisions at the federal level. The memorandum also provided for the continued presence of Russian troops on the territory of the Republic of Moldova for an extended period. Initially, the president at the time, Vladimir Voronin, supported the proposal and was set to sign it in November 2003 in the presence of Russian leader Vladimir Putin. At the last moment, however, Voronin backed away from signing amid opposition protests and discussions with representatives of Western partners. Putin’s visit to Chișinău was cancelled, and the memorandum was never signed. Vladimir Voronin later acknowledged that the Republic of Moldova would have lost its independence had he signed the "Kozak Memorandum." After becoming president in 2016, Igor Dodon continued to advocate for a federal solution to the Transnistrian issue. He also pushed to expand Gagauzia’s powers as part of potential constitutional reform.

editorialRejections.title: Ukraine war latest: Poland plans no-fly zone near Ukraine border, asks NATO to intercept Russian missiles over Ukraine
editorialRejections.summary: Poland plans to establish a no-fly zone along its eastern border with Ukraine by early 2027, Polish officials reported on Nov

editorialRejections.body: Poland plans to establish a no-fly zone along its eastern border with Ukraine by early 2027, Polish officials reported on Nov. 25. The proposals come amid growing concerns over Russian aerial incursions into NATO territory, following a series of incidents involving Russian missiles and drones entering Polish airspace during attacks on Ukraine on Nov. 23 and 24. Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said the planned no-fly zone would extend to over ten kilometers (six miles) from the country's eastern border. The government wants the relevant regulation to take effect by late December or early January, Tomczyk said, according to Polish media . The zone would support a recently introduced procedure that allows Polish pilots to identify and potentially engage aerial targets based on radar information, intelligence from allies, altitude, and speed, rather than requiring visual identification, Tomczyk said. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said on Nov. 25 that shooting down Russian missiles over Ukraine at Kyiv's request could constitute an act of self-defense. Poland has already shot down Russian drones that entered its airspace during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine on Sept. 10, 2025, marking the first time a NATO member engaged Russian aerial targets since the start of the full-scale war. Separately, Warsaw raised the possibility of NATO intercepting Russian missiles over Ukraine during a meeting of alliance ambassadors in Brussels on Nov. 23, Bloomberg reported , citing people familiar with the discussions. Some allies supported the proposal, but the discussions remain preliminary, and no decision has been made yet. Tomczyk said NATO was not supportive of the proposal, citing the complications it would create, and said previous discussions had ruled out such an arrangement, RMF24 reported . Ukrainian forces struck the Syzran and Kuibyshev oil refineries in Russia's Samara Oblast overnight on Nov. 25, the General Staff confirmed. The two oil refineries, both located in Russia's Samara Oblast , are about 100 kilometers (62 miles) apart and are approximately 800 kilometers (500 miles) from Ukraine's border with Russia. The General Staff said the operation was carried out in coordination with "Chernaya Iskra" ("Black Spark" in English), a resistance movement operating inside Russia. The strike on the Kuibyshev oil refinery caused a fire and damaged the AVT-4 and AVT-5 primary oil processing units, a catalytic reforming unit, and two storage tanks, according to the report. The Kuibyshev refinery, one of the largest oil processing facilities in Samara Oblast, is owned by Russia's state-controlled oil giant Rosneft , the General Staff said. A large fire also broke out at the Syzran oil refinery. Preliminary reports indicated that the strike hit the AVT-6 primary oil processing unit, a sulfur treatment unit, a catalytic reforming unit, a hydrotreating unit, an isomerization unit, as well as two storage tanks, the General Staff said. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has detained a former Ukrainian service member suspected of attempting to kill a commander of the Special Operations Forces in the city of Khmelnytskyi, the agency said on Nov. 25. The attempted assassination comes amid a wider shadow war between Russian and Ukrainian intelligence services, which have increasingly used targeted killings and explosives against military and political figures away from the front lines. The suspect, who worked for Russian military intelligence (GRU) , planted an improvised explosive device in his car, which was parked near the building where the targeted commander lived. Acting on orders from Russian intelligence services, he was supposed to detonate the device as the Ukrainian service member walked past the vehicle, the SBU said. The SBU caught the suspect just meters from the planned blast site as he prepared to detonate the homemade bomb with a remote control. The alleged assassination plot also involved a second vehicle fitted with a remotely accessible camera, which Russian intelligence could use to record the explosion. The SBU said Moscow intended to use the footage in information and psychological operations aimed at destabilizing Ukraine. The suspect is a former contract service member from Kharkiv who left the military in 2024 for health reasons. Russian intelligence recruited him through Telegram channels where he had been looking for opportunities to make quick money, the SBU said. He was initially tasked with identifying Ukrainian military infrastructure in Kharkiv, including reserve command posts and vehicle parking areas, before being sent to Khmelnytskyi to prepare the assassination, according to the SBU. To monitor the officer, the suspect allegedly rented an apartment near his home and installed a concealed camera on its balcony to track his daily movements. He later brought a crossover and another vehicle from Kharkiv, fitting the explosive device into the crossover in a rented garage. In exchange for carrying out the killing, his Russian handlers allegedly promised to arrange his evacuation to Russia through third countries and provide him with Russian citizenship, the SBU said. The suspect has been charged with high treason under martial law. He remains in custody without bail and faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property if convicted. A Ukrainian air defense laser has successfully intercepted a Russian jet-powered Geran drone for the first time in combat conditions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Nov. 25. The "Blysk" laser system, deployed by the company Carmine Sky, was protecting a critical infrastructure facility, Beskrestnov said in his statement . At the same time, he managed expectations for the new capability. "It is still too early to talk about serial production of the laser. Tests are underway, during which lasers protect critical infrastructure facilities," he added. Ukraine's deployment of Blysk comes as laser weapons are increasingly being developed as a cheaper alternative to conventional air defense missiles. Among the most prominent examples is Israel's Iron Beam, one of the first high-powered laser air defense systems to enter military service. Ukraine's Blysk has a reported power output of four kilowatts and an effective range of up to one kilometer. So far, persistent cloud cover and fog over Kyiv had reportedly prevented the system from engaging Russian drones effectively. Lasers suffer in poor weather, and cloud cover can disperse the beam before it reaches a drone. On Nov. 19, Carmine Sky announced that Ukraine's first air defense laser was deployed to help protect Kyiv from Russian drones. The laser weapon could offer Ukraine a cheaper way to counter Russian drone attacks, requiring electricity rather than more costly interceptor drones or missiles. But the precision tracking of the target with a laser can be difficult against agile drones. Beskrestnov said that the he technology is being developed within the framework of the "Private Air Defense" state program with the support of the Brave-1 defense technology cluster. Launched by the Defense Ministry, the program authorizes companies to form air defense groups under the Air Force's operational control. Currently, about 100 companies nationwide have joined the effort, with half forming active combat units. These private units use systems ranging from interceptor drones to automated gun turrets. Ukrainian journalists covering a humanitarian mission from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast were outnumbered by Russian propagandists and struggled to transmit their reporting due to limited communications, ICTV correspondent Yehor Romakhlo said, Detector Media said on Nov. 24. The mission took place in late October under a temporary ceasefire negotiated between Ukraine and Russia with the involvement of U.S. first lady Melania Trump. The agreement allowed humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations from Oleshky, a city occupied by Russia since 2022, facing a severe humanitarian crisis. Speaking at a joint meeting of a Ukrainian parliamentary committee and a commission investigating Russian crimes against journalists, Romakhlo described the challenges he faced while covering the operation alongside TSN cameraman Illia Shynkarenko. Romakhlo said he learned about the assignment just four hours before departure, leaving little time to prepare. One of the main obstacles was the lack of reliable communications. The Ukrainian crew had access to a Starlink satellite internet terminal, but it worked for only about half an hour in Oleshky, he said. "It attracted enormous attention from the Russians, both the press and the military. They tried to connect to it and do something with it," Romakhlo said. Russian journalists, by contrast, had reliable internet access throughout the mission, giving them a significant advantage in reporting from the occupied city. "We were traveling on the same bus, and they were putting out material constantly, straight away. We didn't have that opportunity," Romakhlo said. The Ukrainian crew also faced a significant numerical disadvantage, with roughly 30 Russian media representatives covering the mission. The Russian journalists worked together, sharing footage and coordinating their reporting. "I understand the colleagues who, after our return, asked why other media weren't invited," Romakhlo said. "It would have been easier for us to work. We could have joined forces and actually accomplished more." He also described Russian media representatives pushing Ukrainian journalists to the back during joint press encounters with Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova. According to Romakhlo, the Russian side attempted to portray Ukraine as responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, showing visiting journalists what they claimed were Ukrainian mines and drones as evidence. Romakhlo called for better preparation of future humanitarian missions, including advance arrangements for media access, reliable communications, and clearer rules governing journalists' work.

editorialRejections.title: Interview with Becirovic: BiH is an indivisible State; the Messages of ZAVNOBiH should serve as a Guiding Light
