editorialRejections.body: A formal reception was held at the Presidency building of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo to mark Statehood Day. The hosts were Presidency members Denis Bećirović and Darijana Filipović. Filipović, representing the HDZ BiH (Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina), marks the return of officials from that party to the organization of—and attendance at—the Statehood Day reception at the Presidency, following an absence of nearly a decade. Denis Bećirović spoke to the Dnevnik 2 news program of Federalna TV. Member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina Denis Bećirović once again extended his congratulations to all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the occasion of the country’s Statehood Day. “This is one of the most significant dates in our millennial history. It is a date that unites the citizens and peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is nothing controversial about this date. The delegates of ZAVNOBiH [State Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina] represented a multi-ethnic composition. In the midst of the Second World War, they restored the statehood of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They also restored the territorial unity of Bosnia and Herzegovina and delivered a historic lesson for all time,” Bećirović noted. The key message, he stated, is that Bosnia and Herzegovina is an indivisible state. “We in Bosnia and Herzegovina must continue to learn from the ZAVNOBiH delegates. We need to educate younger generations so that they understand the messages and values ​​of ZAVNOBiH.” The messages and values ​​of ZAVNOBiH are not directed against any specific people or any individual, Bećirović added. “The messages of ZAVNOBiH affirm human rights, freedom, and equality. The ZAVNOBiH Declaration on human rights is a magnificent document—not only within the context of Bosnia and Herzegovina but also on a European scale. We must bring this positive legacy to light. We must tell new generations that the future of this country does not lie in chauvinism or hatred, but in unity, cooperation, and in becoming a member of the EU and NATO as soon as possible. Bosnia and Herzegovina is capable of this; however, there are, of course, destructive forces that persistently hinder the country’s path toward EU and NATO membership,” he warned. Bećirović concluded that those who obstruct processes in Bosnia and Herzegovina must be countered “using all legal and political means, in cooperation with our international partners.” When asked how to respond to the denial of the continuity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the blockades of state institutions, Bećirović stated: “During the 2018–2022 term, these very same forces blocked both the European and Euro-Atlantic paths of Bosnia and Herzegovina; consequently, we adopted almost no laws during those four years. In the 2022–2026 term, we have made some significant strides, yet these forces have continued to obstruct our accelerated progress toward the EU and NATO. They persist in threatening such blockades, seemingly unaware that, in doing so, they are causing harm to every single person in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The people of Bosnia and Herzegovina desire a stronger economy, better social protection, social justice, and security for their children. editorialRejections.title: Jordan Parliament debates ‘antiterror’ law after deadly Karak church attack
editorialRejections.summary: The House voted to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law on Wednesday to its Legal Committee for review
editorialRejections.reason: No DNU heading could be identified
editorialRejections.body: Jordan’s Parliament is reviewing proposed amendments to its “antiterrorism” law that would double minimum prison sentences for “terrorism”-related offences after an attack at a church in Karak last month that killed nine people. House of Representatives Speaker Ibrahim Tarawneh said the chamber had pledged to review legislation and consider amendments after the attack at the church in southern Jordan and the killing of a police officer in the capital, Amman. The House voted to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law on Wednesday to its Legal Committee for review. The legislation will return to the chamber for debate and a vote before proceeding to the Senate and, if approved, royal ratification. On October 23, gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority. Authorities said 34 people were wounded. Last week, Jordan’s State Security Court sentenced three men to death for the attack. On Wednesday, the court sentenced another man to death for killing the police officer in Amman. The officer was stabbed while on guard duty near the Sri Lankan embassy on November 5. The government-backed amendments would raise minimum prison terms to 10 years and up to 15 years in certain cases while retaining the death penalty for the most serious offences, the state-run Jordan News Agency reported. The proposed amendments drew criticism from First Deputy Speaker Ayatollah Freihat, who said legislation should not be based on knee-jerk reactions to events, FactJo, a Jordanian news agency, reported. He raised concerns that the amendments could also harm freedom of expression in Jordan. Freihat called on the government to withdraw the draft amendments and form a committee of legal experts to review the state’s criminal policy, criticising the use of “vague” formulations in defining “terrorism”, including “disrupting public order” and “harming the public interest”. Earlier, King Abdullah II had said the kingdom would not be shaken by the attack on the church. Opening the new session of parliament this month, Abdullah said “the treacherous hand of terrorism” had reached out “to test the resilience of our state and the resolve of our people”.

EU Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said the incident was “yet another reminder that security in the Gulf is a matter of security for us all”. “We must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf,” she added.

Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the attack a “blatant breach of international law” and said it “represents a dangerous escalation that could complicate efforts to contain tensions and undermine political and diplomatic efforts.”

The UAE said the “attack constitutes a flagrant violation of the sovereignty of the State of Kuwait and a threat to its security and stability.”

Saudi Arabia said “Iran’s continued attacks mean more tension and destabilisation” that undermine diplomacy in the region.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said, “Iran’s unchecked aggression threatens stability and security in the Middle East and beyond … It must end”.

As we reported earlier, the Iranian armed forces denied carrying out the attack.

editorialRejections.title: Alleged Russian spy goes on trial in Berlin
editorialRejections.body:
A German-Ukrainian businesswoman accused of spying for Russia went on trial Thursday on espionage charges, 10 months after her high-profile arrest sparked a diplomatic clash between Berlin and Moscow.

The start of proceedings in Berlin was postponed after the defendant reported health problems that required medical attention.

She was eventually brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair wearing dark sunglasses, where she was named as Ilona Wiener.

Her lawyers said she would not confirm her personal information and that she was still feeling ill, leading to a further delay.

Wiener, 57, is accused of using contacts with current and former German defence ministry officials to gather information about military aid for Ukraine, drone test sites and the arms industry. In addition, "she is alleged to have maintained contact with a full-time intelligence officer at the Russian Embassy in Berlin," court spokeswoman Lisa Jani told AFP.
